text: Domain Storytelling, by Stefan Hofer and Henning Schwentner (Addison-Wesley, 2021), turns that hour into a model. A domain expert tells one concrete example and a moderator draws it live, in a small pictographic language: story actors (the people and systems that act), work objects (what they act on or pass along: an RFID card, a hold) and activities (arrows labelled with verbs).
author: Stefan Hofer; Henning Schwentner
title: Domain Storytelling: A Collaborative, Visual, and Agile Way to Build Domain-Driven Software
edition: 1st ed., Addison-Wesley Professional, published Sep 7, 2021 (copyright 2022), ISBN 978-0-13-745891-2
locator: ch. 2, "The Pictographic Language" (sections Actors; Work Objects; Activities; Sequence Numbers)

evidence: InformIT TOC: "Chapter 2: The Pictographic Language. Actors; Work Objects; Activities; Sequence Numbers". Quick-start: "The actors' activities are shown as arrows and labeled with verbs from the domain language."; "We usually number the sentences by adding a sequence number to the origin of the arrow that represents an activity."

text: Each story is scoped on three axes (Hofer and Schwentner, ch. 4, "Scope"): granularity (coarse or fine), point in time (as-is or to-be) and domain purity (pure, with only people and paper, or digitalized, with existing systems as story actors).
author: Stefan Hofer; Henning Schwentner
title: Domain Storytelling
locator: ch. 4, "Scope" (Granularity; Point in Time (As-Is vs. To-Be); Domain Purity (Pure vs. Digitalized))

text: His decision heuristic (ch. 10, "Design Heuristics", section "Tactical Design Decision Tree") asks about the logic rather than the label: money, an audit log or deep analytics point to an event-sourced domain model; otherwise complex rules get a domain model, complex data an active record, and the rest a transaction script.
